title: Should we have a fat tax?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss whether a "fat tax" should be imposed to combat obesity. They cover US obesity statistics and healthcare costs, the origins of the fat tax idea (Kelly D. Brown's proposals), three modeled UK/Oxford tax scenarios and their effects on food costs and regressiveness, soda taxes (Richmond, California and other cities), tobacco tax precedent, taxing consumers via insurance instead of food, Japan's Metabo program, public opinion polling, fat taxes in Hungary and Denmark, and a listener mail segment about medical marijuana (Marinol) for children and an iTunes podcast poll.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode with banter about their return from two weeks off, their outfits, and McDonald's menu items in Japan, then introduce the fat tax topic.

segments.title: Obesity statistics and healthcare costs
segments.summary: The hosts cite estimates that obesity costs the US about $150 billion a year in healthcare, that obesity is considered a chronic, preventable disease, and that the obese share of Americans is expected to rise from about a third toward forty percent.

segments.title: Origins of the fat tax idea
segments.summary: The fat tax concept was introduced by Yale psychologist Kelly D. Brown in the New York Times. Brown proposed taxing unhealthy foods and using the revenue to subsidize cheaper healthy foods, and the hosts question whether cheap junk food drives consumption.

segments.title: Oxford study models of food taxes
segments.summary: Oxford University researchers modeled three scenarios: a 17.5 percent value added tax on saturated-fat foods, which could be counterproductive and raise food costs about 3.2 percent; a nutrient-scoring tax that could save about thirty lives a year with a roughly 4 percent cost increase; and a spread-out tax on almost half of foods raising taxes about 4.6 percent. The hosts discuss the regressive nature of food taxes.

segments.title: Soda taxes and existing fat taxes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss existing or proposed soda taxes, including a one-cent-per-ounce tax proposed in Richmond, California, and the regressive effect on cheap store-brand soda. They note California, Maine, and Maryland fat taxes were approved and then repealed, and that Britain taxes some foods already. Hungary and Denmark are also mentioned as having fat taxes, with Denmark taxing saturated fat per kilogram.

segments.title: Tobacco tax precedent and taxing the person via insurance
segments.summary: The hosts compare fat taxes to tobacco taxes, which they say reduced use after prices rose. They then discuss critics' nanny-state objections (Tony Blair called it a sign of a nanny state in 2004) and the alternative of charging obese people higher insurance premiums, comparing it to car insurance and Japan's Metabo program with workplace pressure.

segments.title: Public opinion, shaming, and incentives
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a poll by Phalanx Investment Partners LLC in which one in three Americans favored obese people paying more, with younger and higher-income respondents more supportive. They joke about shaming devices and calorie labels, and mention a gym membership reimbursement offered by their employer.

segments.title: Listener mail: Marinol and iTunes poll
segments.summary: The hosts mention an iTunes podcast popularity poll and read listener mail from a pediatrician (Dr. Jimmy) about Marinol, a synthetic marijuana pill, being used as an antinausea drug for pediatric chemotherapy patients, and the stigma parents attach to it. The hosts close by inviting feedback on social media and email.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing sign-off with contact information and a reminder of the website.
